    All in One View

    Content from Introduction to Data Collection

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 35 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Should I use existing data or collect my own?
    • What kinds of geospatial data will I meet in this module?
    • How can I tell whether a dataset is good enough for my project?

    Objectives

    • Describe the main steps of a data collection workflow
    • Distinguish vector data from raster data
    • Evaluate a dataset using a checklist of quality, license and metadata questions
    • Explain what the FAIR principles mean for data you collect and share

    Why data collection matters

    Every map and every spatial analysis is only as good as the data behind it. For social scientists, the first decision in a project is often the most important one: can I use data that already exists, or do I need to collect my own?

    Pre-existing data is everywhere. Governments publish census statistics, administrative boundaries, roads and land cover. Universities run geoportals full of scanned maps and research datasets. Satellites have photographed the whole planet many times over. Using these sources saves time and money, and makes your work easier for others to repeat.

    But existing data is not always enough. It may be out of date, too coarse, missing the attribute you need, or simply not exist for your topic. Then you collect original data: with a survey, a field visit, interviews, or by digitizing features from maps and imagery.

    The two paths often meet. In the case study used later in this module, we take census data and road data from government sources, then add grocery store locations that could be checked or collected in the field, because no official list says where every store is, what it sells, and whether it accepts SNAP benefits.

    What this module covers

    Episode Kind of data Tools
    Finding Data in Repositories Vector data from geoportals and open data hubs Web browser, QGIS
    Data from the U.S. Census Bureau Census boundaries and statistics Web browser, Python (Colab)
    Acquiring Imagery Scanned maps and satellite imagery (raster) Web browser, QGIS
    Collecting Data in the Field Original observations QField, QGIS
    QField demonstration Mapping grocery stores QField, QGIS
    Network Analysis for Grocery Access Using the collected data QGIS

    Vector and raster data

    Geospatial data comes in two basic forms.

    • Vector data stores features as points (a store), lines (a road) or polygons (a city boundary), each with a row of attributes in a table. Census boundaries, roads and field observations are vector data.
    • Raster data is a grid of cells (pixels), each holding a value: a color, an elevation, a land cover class, a temperature. Satellite images, scanned maps and elevation models are rasters.
    Vector Raster
    Represents Discrete features with clear edges Continuous surfaces, or images
    Examples Tracts, roads, stores, survey points Satellite images, elevation, land cover
    Detail Set by the precision of coordinates Set by the cell size (resolution)
    Common formats GeoJSON, shapefile, GeoPackage GeoTIFF, JPEG2000, NetCDF

    Neither is better; they answer different questions, and many projects use both. A satellite image (raster) might be traced to create building outlines (vector), and census tracts (vector) might be used to summarize a land cover map (raster).

    Is this dataset good enough?

    Before you build a project on someone else’s data, ask:

    Question Why it matters
    Who made it, and how? A government survey, a crowd-sourced map and a student project differ in method and reliability
    When? Boundaries, roads and stores change. Is it recent enough for your question?
    Where, and at what detail? Coverage, resolution or scale must match your study area and question
    What exactly is measured? Read the definitions. “Grocery store” or “household” may not mean what you assume
    How accurate is it? Look for margins of error, positional accuracy and known gaps
    What coordinate system? You will need it to line layers up correctly
    Can I use it? Check the license: some data is public domain, some requires credit, some cannot be shared

    Most of these answers are in the dataset’s metadata: the documentation that describes the data. Data without metadata is a warning sign.

    FAIR data

    When you collect or share data yourself, aim to make it FAIR:

    • Findable: it has a clear name, a description and, ideally, a persistent identifier such as a DOI
    • Accessible: others can retrieve it, for example from a repository, even if access is controlled
    • Interoperable: it uses common formats and standard codes (GeoJSON, GEOIDs, EPSG codes)
    • Reusable: it has a license, a description of methods, and enough metadata for someone else to use it correctly

    Field data that sits in one person’s phone, with column names only they understand, is none of these things. The QField episodes show how a planned form, consistent categories and good notes make field data reusable.

    Challenge

    Existing data or new data?

    For each research question, decide whether you would start with existing data, collect your own, or both. Name a possible source.

    1. How has median household income changed in Indiana counties since 2015?
    2. Which bus stops in your city have a bench and a shelter?
    3. How much forest was lost around a national park between 1970 and today?
    1. Existing data. The American Community Survey publishes median household income for every county every year (Data from the U.S. Census Bureau episode).
    2. Probably both. A transit agency may publish stop locations, but amenities such as benches are often missing or out of date, so you would check them in the field.
    3. Existing imagery. Declassified CORONA images (1960 to 1972) and modern Landsat or Sentinel-2 images can be compared (Acquiring Imagery episode). You might verify a sample of areas in the field.
    Challenge

    Vector or raster?

    Would each of these usually be stored as vector or raster data?

    1. Locations of public libraries
    2. Air temperature across a state
    3. School district boundaries
    4. A scanned 1890 city map
    1. Vector (points)
    2. Raster (a continuous surface)
    3. Vector (polygons)
    4. Raster (an image), until you trace features from it into vector layers
    Key Points
    • Start every project by asking whether suitable data already exists
    • Vector data stores discrete features; raster data stores values in a grid of cells
    • Check who made a dataset, when, how, at what detail, with what accuracy, and under what license
    • Make the data you collect FAIR: findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable

    Content from Finding Data in Repositories

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 35 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Where can I find free vector data for my project?
    • How do I judge whether a downloaded dataset is trustworthy?
    • Can QGIS read data straight from the web?

    Objectives

    • Name several types of geospatial data repositories and what each is good for
    • Search a geoportal and read a dataset’s metadata
    • Load a vector dataset into QGIS directly from a web address

    Pre-existing vector data

    Vector data for natural features, political boundaries, transportation networks and many other topics already exists somewhere on the web, so you rarely have to create it from scratch. Many datasets are free on government, university and open-source websites; some specialized datasets are sold. Quality varies widely with the methods used to make them, so explore each dataset and its metadata before you rely on it.

    Kinds of repositories

    Kind What you find there Examples
    National statistical agencies Official boundaries and statistics U.S. Census Bureau (next episode)
    State and local open data portals Parcels, roads, zoning, schools, local boundaries IndianaMap, city and county GIS portals
    University geoportals Research datasets and scanned maps collected by libraries Big Ten Academic Alliance Geoportal, GeoData@Tufts
    Open data hubs Datasets published by many organizations in one search Esri ArcGIS Hub
    Global open datasets Consistent data for the whole world Natural Earth, OpenStreetMap, HydroSHEDS
    Thematic repositories Data on one subject, often linked to surveys DHS Program Spatial Data Repository

    A starting list

    Explore these sources. Bookmark the ones that seem most useful for your teaching or research. Data sources specific to your area are usually on your state or local government’s website.

    Source What it offers
    Big Ten Academic Alliance Geoportal Search across the GIS data and scanned maps held by Big Ten universities, including Purdue
    GeoData@Tufts Search, preview and download geospatial data from several university repositories
    IndianaMap Indiana’s statewide GIS data: boundaries, roads, imagery, geology, infrastructure and more
    Esri ArcGIS Hub Open datasets published by governments and organizations that use Esri software
    Natural Earth Free country, state, coastline and city layers for the whole world, at three map scales
    Geofabrik OpenStreetMap downloads OpenStreetMap data (roads, buildings, points of interest) cut into regions
    HydroSHEDS Global rivers, lakes and watershed boundaries
    DHS Spatial Data Repository Boundaries and survey indicators from the Demographic and Health Surveys in more than 90 countries
    Callout

    Read the license

    “Free to download” does not always mean “free to reuse”. U.S. federal data such as Census files is public domain. OpenStreetMap data is free under the Open Database License, which requires you to credit “OpenStreetMap contributors”. Some university and commercial data may only be used by members of an institution. The license is usually on the dataset’s metadata page.

    Reading metadata

    Every good repository shows a metadata page for each dataset. When you open one, look for:

    • Title, author or publisher, and a date (of the data, not just of the upload)
    • An abstract or description of what is included
    • The spatial extent (where it covers) and scale or resolution
    • The coordinate reference system
    • The attributes (columns) and what they mean
    • Lineage: how the data was created and processed
    • The license or use constraints

    Loading data straight from the web

    You do not always have to download a file before using it. QGIS can open a file directly from its web address. Let us load the Natural Earth countries layer this way.

    1. In QGIS, go to Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer.
    2. For Source Type, choose Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc.
    3. Leave Type as HTTP/HTTPS/FTP and paste this address into URI: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvkelso/natural-earth-vector/master/geojson/ne_110m_admin_0_countries.geojson
    4. Click Add, then Close.

    The world’s countries appear. Right-click the layer and choose Open Attribute Table to see its attributes, such as NAME, CONTINENT and POP_EST. The rest of this module uses this method to load the lesson data, so you never have to manage downloaded files.

    Challenge

    Explore a geoportal

    1. Open the Big Ten Academic Alliance Geoportal and search for Tippecanoe.
    2. Pick one result and open its record.
    3. Answer: Who published it? What year does the data describe? What format can you download? Is there a license or use statement?

    Results change over time, but you will typically find county layers from IndianaMap and the Census Bureau, scanned historical maps from university libraries, and aerial imagery. A good record lists the publisher, the date of the data, the formats available (for example shapefile, GeoJSON or a web service) and a rights statement. If a record is missing several of these, treat the data with caution.

    Challenge

    Which source would you use?

    Which source from the list above would you try first for each of these?

    1. River networks for a study of flooding in Bangladesh
    2. Country outlines for a world map in a slide presentation
    3. Indiana school district boundaries
    4. All cafes in Chicago
    1. HydroSHEDS, which covers the whole world consistently
    2. Natural Earth, designed for small-scale maps like this
    3. IndianaMap, or the Census Bureau’s school district boundaries
    4. OpenStreetMap through Geofabrik (search for amenity=cafe). Coverage depends on local volunteers, so check it against another source
    Key Points
    • Search existing repositories before creating data from scratch
    • Different repositories serve different needs: official statistics, local data, research collections, global layers
    • Read the metadata and the license before you use a dataset
    • QGIS can open data directly from a web address, so you do not need to download files

    Content from Data from the U.S. Census Bureau

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 65 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What data does the U.S. Census Bureau publish, and how is it organized?
    • What is the difference between the Decennial Census and the American Community Survey?
    • How do I get census data with the Census API?
    • How do census tables connect to census maps?

    Objectives

    • Describe the three main Census Bureau products: boundary files, the Decennial Census and the ACS
    • Explain census geographies and how GEOIDs identify them
    • Interpret ACS estimates together with their margins of error
    • Build a Census API request and run it in a web browser
    • Use the Python notebooks to download census data and join it to boundaries

    Introduction

    The U.S. Census Bureau is the largest source of free social and economic data about the United States. Social scientists use it to describe neighborhoods, plan services for particular groups, choose sites for new facilities, study the effects of policies and hazards, and much more. Three products matter most for mapping:

    1. Boundary files (TIGER/Line and cartographic boundary files): the shapes
    2. The Decennial Census: a count of everyone, every ten years
    3. The American Community Survey (ACS): a yearly survey with detailed social and economic topics

    Census geography

    The Census Bureau reports data for a hierarchy of areas. Each level nests inside the one above:

    Level Typical size Example in Tippecanoe County
    State Indiana
    County Tippecanoe County
    Census tract about 1,200 to 8,000 people (4,000 on average) 43 tracts
    Block group about 600 to 3,000 people Several per tract
    Block A city block, or a larger rural area Smallest unit; Decennial Census only

    Other geographies do not nest neatly: places (cities and towns), ZIP Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs, approximations of ZIP code areas), congressional districts, school districts and urban areas.

    Every area has a GEOID built from FIPS codes (Federal Information Processing Standards codes):

    Level Pattern Example Meaning
    State SS 18 Indiana
    County SS + CCC 18157 Tippecanoe County
    Tract SS + CCC + TTTTTT 18157010600 Tract 106
    Block group tract + G 181570106001 Block group 1 of tract 106

    GEOIDs are text, not numbers. If a program stores 01 (Alabama) as the number 1, it no longer matches, which is the most common reason a table fails to join to a map.

    Boundary files

    The shapes come in two families:

    • TIGER/Line files (named tl_...) are the full-detail master files, published every year since 2007. They include legal boundaries that extend into water, and features such as roads, railroads and rivers.
    • Cartographic boundary files (named cb_...) are simplified versions clipped to the shoreline, at 1:500,000, 1:5,000,000 and 1:20,000,000 scale. They are much smaller and are the better choice for thematic maps.

    Both are free from https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files.html and can be read straight from the web by QGIS or Python.

    The Decennial Census and the American Community Survey

    The Decennial Census counts every person living in the United States every ten years (most recently in 2020). Because it is a count, it has no sampling error, but it asks only a few questions: age, sex, race, Hispanic origin, household relationship, and whether a home is owned or rented. It is published down to the block level.

    The American Community Survey (ACS) is sent to about 3.5 million addresses every year. It covers topics the Decennial Census does not, including:

    • Social: school enrollment, educational attainment, marital status, veteran status, disability, language spoken at home, ancestry, place of birth
    • Economic: income, poverty, employment, occupation, commuting, SNAP benefits, health insurance
    • Housing: home value, rent, vehicles available, internet access, year built
    American Community Survey Decennial Census
    Method Survey of a sample Count of everyone
    How often Every year Every 10 years
    Topics Many social, economic and housing topics A few basic topics
    Margins of error Yes No
    Smallest area Block group (5-year estimates) Block

    1-year and 5-year estimates

    Product Based on Published for Best when
    1-year estimates 12 months of responses Areas with 65,000 or more people You need the most current numbers for a large area
    5-year estimates 60 months of responses All areas, down to block groups You need small areas or more reliable numbers

    The “2024 ACS 5-year estimates” pool responses from 2020 to 2024. They describe that whole period, not the year 2024 alone. (A 3-year product also existed, but it was discontinued after the 2011 to 2013 release.)

    Margins of error

    Because the ACS is a sample, every number is an estimate with a margin of error (MOE). The Census Bureau publishes 90% margins of error: we can be 90% confident the true value lies within the estimate plus or minus the MOE.

    Notice that large counties have narrow error bars and small counties have wide ones. Blackford County’s 9.5% could plausibly be anywhere from about 6% to 13%. Two estimates whose ranges overlap a lot may not really be different. A common rule of thumb uses the coefficient of variation (CV), the standard error as a percentage of the estimate:

    CV = (MOE / 1.645) / estimate x 100

    A CV below 12% is usually considered highly reliable, 12% to 40% medium, and above 40% low.

    Callout

    Why is LaGrange County so high?

    LaGrange County in northern Indiana is home to one of the largest Amish communities in the United States, and many Amish households do not own cars. Surprising values often have real explanations. Look for them before you assume the data is wrong.

    Three ways to get census data

    Method Good for
    data.census.gov Browsing and downloading a table or two by clicking
    Census Data API Asking for exactly the variables and places you need, from a browser or a program; reproducible
    Bulk files (FTP) Downloading everything for a product at once

    The rest of this episode uses the API.

    The Census Data API

    An API (Application Programming Interface) lets you request data with a web address instead of clicking through a website. The answer comes back as a table (in JSON or CSV format) that a program can read directly. The API only ever returns summary data for areas, never information about individual people.

    Callout

    You need a free API key

    The Census API now requires a key with every request. Without one it replies with a “Missing Key” page. Request a key at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html. It arrives by email within a few minutes, and you must click the activation link in that email before it works. In the examples below, replace YOUR_KEY with your own key. Treat it like a password and do not post it online.

    Anatomy of a request 

    https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/profile?get=NAME,DP04_0058E&for=county:*&in=state:18&key=YOUR_KEY
    Part In the example Meaning
    Dataset 2024/acs/acs5/profile 2024 ACS 5-year estimates, data profile tables
    get= NAME,DP04_0058E The variables you want, separated by commas
    for= county:* The geography; * means all of them
    in= state:18 The area they are inside (Indiana)
    key= YOUR_KEY Your API key

    The parts after the ? are joined with &. Paste the address (with your key) into a web browser and you will see a list of rows, one per county:

    [["NAME","DP04_0058E","state","county"],
 ["Adams County, Indiana","1626","18","001"],
 ...

    Step 1: Find a dataset

    The list of all datasets is at https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets.html. Some common ones:

    Dataset path What it is
    2024/acs/acs5 ACS 5-year detailed tables (variables starting with B or C)
    2024/acs/acs5/profile ACS 5-year data profiles (DP): ready-made counts and percentages
    2024/acs/acs5/subject ACS 5-year subject tables (S)
    2024/acs/acs1 ACS 1-year detailed tables (areas of 65,000 or more people)
    2020/dec/dp 2020 Decennial Census demographic profile

    Step 2: Find your variables

    Every dataset has a variables page. Add /variables.html to the dataset address, for example https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/profile/variables.html. Press Ctrl+F (or Cmd+F on a Mac) and search for words such as “no vehicles available”. You will find:

    Variable Label
    DP04_0058E Estimate: occupied housing units with no vehicles available
    DP04_0058M Margin of error of that estimate
    DP04_0058PE Percent of occupied housing units with no vehicles available
    DP04_0058PM Margin of error of that percent

    The last letters tell you what a variable is: E is an estimate, M its margin of error, and in the data profiles PE and PM are the percent and its margin of error. Variable names are case-sensitive.

    Step 3: Choose the geography

    You want Use
    All states for=state:*
    All counties in Indiana for=county:*&in=state:18
    One county for=county:157&in=state:18
    All tracts in one county for=tract:*&in=state:18&in=county:157
    All tracts in a state for=tract:*&in=state:18

    Tract and block group requests must name a state. State FIPS codes are listed at https://www.census.gov/library/reference/code-lists/ansi.html.

    Step 4: Optional extras

    • Add &descriptive=true to get a second header row with each variable’s plain-language label.
    • Add &outputFormat=csv to get a CSV file instead of JSON, which opens in Excel.

    For example, this returns the number and percent of households without a vehicle for Tippecanoe County as a CSV file:

    https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/profile?get=NAME,DP04_0058E,DP04_0058PE&for=county:157&in=state:18&outputFormat=csv&key=YOUR_KEY
    Callout

    Special values

    Sometimes the API returns large negative numbers such as -666666666. These are annotation codes, not real values. -666666666 means the estimate could not be calculated, often because too few people were sampled, or because almost everyone in the area lives in group quarters (such as university residence halls or prisons), which are not households. Replace them with “missing” before calculating.

    The Census Bureau also has a short video: Using the API to Access Census Data.

    Hands-on: the Python notebooks

    Three Google Colab notebooks put all of this into practice. They read every file straight from the web, so there is nothing to download. Notebooks 1b and 1c need your Census API key.

    Notebook What you will do Open
    1a. Census Boundaries Read TIGER/Line and cartographic boundary files, find FIPS codes, map counties, tracts and roads Open in Colab
    1b. Census API Basics Make API requests, look up variables, use margins of error, compare the ACS and the Decennial Census Open in Colab
    1c. Joining Tables to Maps Join ACS data to tract boundaries by GEOID and map households without a car, showing reliability Open in Colab

    In Colab, choose File > Save a copy in Drive first so your changes are kept.

    Notebook 1c ends with this map:

    The highest shares are in central Lafayette and West Lafayette, where many residents are students or live in apartments within walking distance of shops and bus routes. Tract 104, on the Purdue campus, has more than 8,000 residents but no households, because nearly everyone there lives in residence halls. Hatched tracts have estimates with low reliability.

    Challenge

    Read a GEOID

    What does the GEOID 181570104002 identify?

    It has 12 characters, so it is a block group: state 18 (Indiana), county 157 (Tippecanoe), tract 010400 (tract 104), block group 2.

    Challenge

    Build an API request

    Write a Census API address that returns total population (B01003_001E) and its margin of error for every county in Ohio (state FIPS code 39) from the 2024 ACS 5-year detailed tables. Then open it in your browser with your key.

    https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5?get=NAME,B01003_001E,B01003_001M&for=county:*&in=state:39&key=YOUR_KEY

    Detailed tables (variables starting with B) use the dataset path 2024/acs/acs5, without /profile. Ohio has 88 counties, so you should see 89 rows including the header.

    Challenge

    Are these really different?

    Two neighboring counties report these shares of households without a vehicle:

    • County A: 6.0%, margin of error 2.5
    • County B: 4.5%, margin of error 2.7

    Can you say County A has a higher rate than County B?

    Not with confidence. County A’s range is 3.5% to 8.5% and County B’s is 1.8% to 7.2%. The ranges overlap a lot, so the difference may just be sampling noise. (The Census Bureau publishes a formal significance test for comparing two estimates, but overlapping ranges are a quick warning sign.)

    Key Points
    • Census boundary files provide the shapes; the Decennial Census and the ACS provide the numbers
    • GEOIDs link tables to shapes; keep them as text
    • The Decennial Census is a full count with few questions; the ACS is a yearly survey with many topics and margins of error
    • Use 5-year ACS estimates for small areas, and always check margins of error
    • The Census API needs a free key and lets you request exactly the variables and places you need

    Content from Acquiring Imagery: Scanned Maps and Satellite Data

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 50 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • Where can I find historic maps and satellite imagery?
    • What is the difference between a scanned map and a georeferenced image?
    • How do I find and download declassified CORONA and Sentinel-2 imagery?

    Objectives

    • Explain spatial, spectral and temporal resolution
    • Download a scanned historic map from a library collection
    • Search for and download CORONA imagery from the CAST atlas and USGS EarthExplorer
    • Search for and download Sentinel-2 imagery from the Copernicus Browser
    • Open a downloaded image in QGIS

    Introduction

    Paper maps, air photos and other images scanned at high resolution are often georeferenced (given real coordinates) so they can sit under other layers in a GIS. Features in them, such as old buildings, roads or field boundaries, can then be digitized into vector layers for analysis. Satellite images add a view of the whole landscape, often repeated over time.

    Many websites offer this kind of raster data for free:

    • Scanned historic maps are usually plain images with no coordinates. You must georeference them before use. (See the section on georeferencing in the Data Management module.)
    • Modern satellite imagery is already georeferenced and can be opened directly.
    • Some sources are offered as web services that QGIS can display without downloading anything.

    Resolution: three kinds

    Kind Question it answers Example
    Spatial resolution How large is one pixel on the ground? Sentinel-2: 10 m; Landsat color bands: 30 m; best CORONA: about 2 m (6 feet)
    Spectral resolution How many wavelength bands, and which? A photograph has 3 (red, green, blue); Sentinel-2 has 13, including near-infrared
    Temporal resolution How often is the same place imaged? Sentinel-2: about every 5 days; CORONA: occasional missions from 1960 to 1972

    Higher spatial resolution shows smaller objects; more spectral bands help tell vegetation, water, soil and buildings apart; frequent revisits let you track change.

    Sources

    • Perry-Castañeda Library Map Collection, University of Texas: thousands of scanned maps, free to download
    • Old Maps Online: a search engine across many map libraries, by place and date
    • National Library of Australia Trove: digitized maps, photographs and newspapers
    • University library collections, such as those found through the Big Ten Academic Alliance Geoportal
    • USGS EarthExplorer: Landsat, declassified CORONA imagery, aerial photos and elevation data, including the SRTM 30 m elevation model
    • Copernicus Browser: Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2 and other European satellite data
    • CORONA Atlas, University of Arkansas CAST: CORONA images that have already been georeferenced
    • OpenTopography: elevation data, including SRTM and high-resolution lidar

    Part 1: Download a historic map (beginner)

    The University of Texas Perry-Castañeda Library (PCL) Map Collection hosts thousands of scanned paper maps, organized by region and country.

    1. Go to https://maps.lib.utexas.edu/maps/.
    2. Open the Historical Maps section (or browse a region).
    3. Browse until you find a useful map. Large series, such as military topographic maps, often have index maps that help you find the sheet for a particular area.
    4. To save a map, right-click it and choose Save Image As, and save it in your project folder.
    5. Note where the map came from: title, date, publisher and the page address. You will need these to cite it.

    The saved file is an ordinary image. To use it with other layers, you must georeference it in QGIS (Layer > Georeferencer) by matching points on the map to known coordinates.

    Part 2: Declassified CORONA imagery (intermediate)

    During the Cold War, the United States ran a series of secret photo reconnaissance satellites. The CORONA program (1960 to 1972) produced more than 860,000 black-and-white images, the first satellite photographs of much of the Earth’s surface. The images were declassified in 1995. The best of them, from the KH-4B cameras (1967 to 1972), show objects as small as about 6 feet (2 m), and were taken as overlapping stereo pairs on long, narrow film strips, each covering a strip of ground well over 100 km long.

    CORONA images have become a valuable record of landscapes before modern urban growth, dam building and industrial farming. Archaeologists, historians and geographers use them to find ancient sites, old field systems, and settlements that have since disappeared.

    2a. Georeferenced CORONA images from CAST

    The CORONA Atlas & Referencing System, run by the University of Arkansas Center for Advanced Spatial Technologies (CAST), offers CORONA images that have already been georeferenced, free of charge. It does not cover the whole world, but it is a good first place to look.

    1. Go to https://corona.cast.uark.edu/ and click Explore Atlas.
    2. Red outlines show the areas covered by CORONA missions in the atlas. Zoom in to one of them.
    3. Use the slider at the bottom of the screen to compare CORONA with modern imagery side by side.
    4. Expand the Corona Imagery layer with the + button to see the images being displayed. As you zoom in, the list gets shorter.
    5. Turn images on and off to choose the one you want, then click the blue down-arrow next to it to download it. The files are large, so this can take a while.
    6. Move the file from your Downloads folder to a project folder, for example GIS/CORONA.
    7. In QGIS, go to Layer > Add Layer > Add Raster Layer, browse to the file and click Add.

    2b. Raw CORONA scans from USGS EarthExplorer

    USGS EarthExplorer holds the complete CORONA collection. Its images are not georeferenced, and the interface takes some getting used to, but it covers far more of the world.

    1. Log in, or create a free account, at https://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/.
    2. In the map on the right, navigate to your area of interest. Either click to draw a polygon around it, or zoom to it and press Use Map in the Search Criteria tab.
    3. In the Data Sets tab, expand Declassified Data and check Declass 1 (1996).
    4. In the Additional Criteria tab, set Camera Resolution to Stereo High. This keeps only the high-quality KH-4B images.
    5. Optionally, set Download Availability to Yes to show only images that are already scanned. Unscanned frames can be scanned on request for a fee ($30 per frame at the time of writing).
    6. Click Results.
    7. Use the Footprint and Image Overlay icons to see where each image falls. The Show Metadata and Browse icon opens a preview, where you can check for clouds and clarity.
    8. When you have chosen an image, click the Download Options icon and download it.

    The download is a compressed archive (.tgz). Extract it (on Windows, with a tool such as 7-Zip, you may need to extract twice: first the .tgz, then the .tar inside it). Because each film strip is so long, the image is usually split into several .tif files ending in a, b, c and d. You will need to georeference them before use.

    Part 3: Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery (intermediate)

    Sentinel-2 is part of the European Union’s Copernicus Earth observation program. Since 2015 its satellites (Sentinel-2A and 2B, joined by 2C, launched in 2024) have imaged all land surfaces about every 5 days in 13 spectral bands, at 10 m, 20 m and 60 m resolution. They are used to map land cover, crops, forests, water, urban growth and disaster damage. The data is free.

    Compared with the 30 m color bands of Landsat, Sentinel-2’s 10 m bands show much more detail. Commercial imagery (such as that in Google Earth) can be sharper still, but Sentinel-2’s extra bands, especially near-infrared, and its frequent revisits make it well suited to studying change over time.

    Find and preview imagery

    1. Open the Copernicus Browser and log in, or create a free account with the Register button.
    2. Zoom the map to your area of interest.
    3. The panel on the left has two tabs, Visualize and Search. In Visualize, choose a date (days with imagery are highlighted in the calendar) or click Show latest date, and limit cloud cover with the slider.
    4. Choose a layer, such as True color, False color (vegetation shows red) or NDVI (a vegetation index), to view different band combinations.

    Search and download

    1. Open the Search tab. Choose Sentinel-2, then MSI, then L2A (surface reflectance, already corrected for the atmosphere).
    2. Set a time range and click Search. Each result is shown as an outline on the map; hovering over a result highlights it.
    3. Click the i button on a result to see its details, including cloud cover.
    4. To download, click the download icon next to the result. The file size is shown, and large products can take a while.

    The download is a .SAFE.zip file. Unzip it; the individual bands are stored as .jp2 image files inside the GRANULE/.../IMG_DATA folders, and QGIS can open them with Add Raster Layer.

    Callout

    Too big to download?

    A single Sentinel-2 product is often 500 MB to 1 GB. Download only what you need: in the Copernicus Browser you can also download a single band file, or export just the visible area as an image. The Data Analysis module’s NDVI notebooks show how to work with satellite bands in Python.

    Challenge

    Find a historic map

    Using the PCL Map Collection or Old Maps Online, find a map of your hometown (or of Lafayette, Indiana) made before 1950. Note its title, date, scale and publisher.

    Answers will vary. A good record of a map includes its title, date, scale (for example 1:24,000), publisher, the collection that holds it, and the web address. Old Maps Online lets you filter by date with a slider, and shows each map’s footprint on a modern map.

    Challenge

    Download a CORONA image

    Find a CORONA image of your area of interest, or of a famous landmark, in the CAST atlas. If the atlas does not cover it, search EarthExplorer instead. Then open the image in QGIS.

    The CAST atlas does not cover every area; if yours is missing, EarthExplorer holds the complete collection. An image from CAST lines up with other layers immediately; an image from EarthExplorer appears without coordinates until you georeference it.

    Challenge

    Which source?

    Which imagery source would you use for each task?

    1. Comparing farmland around a Middle Eastern village in 1968 and today
    2. Mapping where crops were stressed by drought in Indiana last summer
    3. Showing what downtown Lafayette looked like in 1900
    1. CORONA for 1968 (try CAST first), and Sentinel-2 or modern high-resolution imagery for today
    2. Sentinel-2: frequent revisits and a near-infrared band for vegetation indices such as NDVI
    3. A scanned historic map, such as a Sanborn fire insurance map, from a library collection
    Key Points
    • Raster data includes scanned maps (which need georeferencing) and satellite images (already georeferenced)
    • Consider spatial, spectral and temporal resolution when choosing imagery
    • Declassified CORONA images (1960 to 1972) are a free historical record; CAST offers georeferenced copies
    • Sentinel-2 provides free 10 m multispectral imagery about every 5 days, from the Copernicus Browser

    Content from Collecting Data in the Field

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 40 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • When should I collect my own geospatial data?
    • How do I design a form so that field data is consistent and easy to analyze?
    • How accurate is GPS on a phone, and why does it matter?
    • What ethical questions come with collecting data about people and places?

    Objectives

    • Name common methods and apps for field data collection
    • Design a data schema with clear fields, data types and dropdown choices
    • Explain the main sources of GPS error and how to record accuracy
    • Plan for consent, privacy and safety before going into the field

    Why collect your own data?

    Existing datasets rarely describe exactly what a social scientist needs. A city may publish where bus stops are, but not whether they have shelters. A business list may include grocery stores, but not whether they sell fresh produce or accept SNAP benefits. When the data you need does not exist, is out of date, or cannot be trusted, you collect it yourself.

    Common methods include:

    Method What you record Example
    Observation Features and their condition, at a location Sidewalk condition, store amenities, vacant lots
    Surveys and interviews People’s answers, often linked to a place Where residents shop, and how they get there
    Participatory mapping Places people draw or point to Areas residents consider unsafe, or important
    Digitizing Features traced from maps or imagery Buildings visible on a CORONA image
    Sensors Measurements at locations Air quality, noise, temperature

    Apps for field data collection

    Most field data is now collected on a phone or tablet, with forms that record a location automatically.

    App Notes
    QField Free and open source; uses projects prepared in QGIS; works offline; Android, iOS, Windows, macOS and Linux
    Mergin Maps Also based on QGIS projects, with built-in syncing
    KoboToolbox and ODK Free survey tools widely used in research and humanitarian work; strong for questionnaires, with GPS points
    ArcGIS Field Maps and Survey123 Esri’s apps; require an ArcGIS account, which many universities provide

    This module uses QField, because it is free and works directly with QGIS. The next episode walks through a complete QField project.

    Design the data before you collect it

    Field data collection fails most often not in the field, but at the desk beforehand. If every person invents their own categories, the result cannot be analyzed. Before anyone goes out, decide on a schema: the list of fields, their types and their allowed values.

    Field Type Allowed values Why
    store_name Text To identify and de-duplicate stores
    store_type Dropdown Supermarket, Convenience, Small market, Other So stores can be compared and filtered
    snap_accepted Dropdown Yes, No, Unknown Access for people using benefits
    produce_available Dropdown Yes, No, Unknown A simple measure of healthy food
    photo Attachment Evidence for checking later
    notes Text Anything unusual, without inventing new fields

    Good practice:

    • Use dropdowns (also called domains or value maps) wherever possible. Free text produces “SNAP”, “snap”, “EBT” and “yes” for the same thing.
    • Always include Unknown. Guessing introduces bias; “Unknown” is honest.
    • Make essential fields required, so a record cannot be saved without them.
    • Write a placement rule for points, for example “stand at the main public entrance”. Without one, some people will mark the middle of the building and others the parking lot.
    • Use short, lowercase field names without spaces (snap_accepted, not SNAP Accepted?). They work in every program.
    • Test the form on a few real sites before the full collection.

    How accurate is GPS?

    Phones use GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite Systems: GPS, Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou) to find their position. Under open sky a modern phone is usually accurate to about 3 to 5 meters, but accuracy gets much worse:

    • next to tall buildings, which block satellites and bounce signals (called multipath)
    • under dense trees
    • indoors
    • in the first moments after the app starts, before enough satellites are found

    Field apps such as QField show the current accuracy as a circle around your position and a number in meters. Wait until it settles, set a target (for example, under 10 m), and record the accuracy with every point. External GNSS receivers can reach sub-meter or even centimeter accuracy, at extra cost.

    Does a few meters matter? For counting stores in a county, rarely. For measuring walking distance to a store entrance, or deciding which side of a boundary a store is on, it can.

    Ethics, privacy and safety

    Collecting data about places often means collecting data about people. Before you start:

    • Get approval. Research with human participants (surveys, interviews, photos of people) usually needs review by your institution’s Institutional Review Board (IRB).
    • Ask for consent, and explain how the data will be used and shared.
    • Protect privacy. A precise location can identify a person or a household. Avoid recording home locations unless you must; if you do, store them securely, and share only aggregated or generalized versions.
    • Respect property and people. Stay on public land unless you have permission. Do not photograph people without consent.
    • Stay safe. Work in pairs, tell someone your route, and carry a charged phone.
    • Keep field notes. Record the date, the team, the weather, problems and decisions. They become part of your metadata.

    Check the data quickly (quality assurance)

    Review the data the same day while you still remember what you saw:

    1. Completeness: are required fields filled in?
    2. Location: do points fall where they should, inside the study area?
    3. Duplicates: is the same place recorded twice?
    4. Consistency: are categories used the same way by everyone?
    5. Evidence: do photos match their records?
    Challenge

    Design a schema

    You are mapping bus stops in your city to study accessibility for wheelchair users. List five fields you would collect, with their type and allowed values.

    One possible schema:

    Field Type Allowed values
    stop_id Text Code shown on the stop sign, to match the transit agency’s data
    shelter Dropdown Yes, No, Unknown
    bench Dropdown Yes, No, Unknown
    curb_ramp Dropdown Yes, No, Unknown
    surface Dropdown Paved pad, Grass or dirt, Other
    photo Attachment
    notes Text

    A placement rule, such as “stand at the stop sign”, keeps the points consistent.

    Challenge

    Spot the problems

    Three volunteers mapped the same neighborhood. Here are some of their records:

    store_name store_type snap_accepted gps_accuracy_m
    Fresh Foods supermarket yes 4
    Fresh Foods Market Supermarket EBT 6
    Corner Stop gas station 38

    What problems can you find, and how would a better form have prevented them?

    • The first two rows are probably the same store entered twice with different names. A QA check for nearby points with similar names would find it.
    • store_type uses inconsistent capitalization and a category (“gas station”) that is not on the list. A dropdown prevents both.
    • snap_accepted has “yes” and “EBT”, and one blank. A Yes, No, Unknown dropdown, made required, fixes this.
    • An accuracy of 38 m is poor. The volunteer should have waited for a better fix, or written a note.
    Key Points
    • Collect your own data when what you need does not exist or cannot be trusted
    • Design the schema first: clear fields, dropdowns, an “Unknown” option and a placement rule
    • Phone GPS is typically accurate to a few meters under open sky, and much worse near buildings and trees; record accuracy
    • Plan for consent, privacy and safety before collecting data about people and places
    • Check data the same day it is collected

    Content from QField Demonstration: Mapping Grocery Stores

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 45 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • What does a QField data collection project look like from start to finish?
    • What should we record at each grocery store to support a later food access analysis?
    • How do we keep field data consistent and ready for quality checks?

    Objectives

    • Follow an end-to-end field workflow, using grocery stores in Lafayette and West Lafayette as the example
    • Explain the reasons behind point placement, attribute choices and GPS accuracy rules
    • Recognize what good field data looks like before collecting it yourself

    Scenario

    Imagine you are on a community research team in Lafayette and West Lafayette, Indiana. Your goal is to understand where access to groceries may be limited, so that you can later map potential food deserts using demographic data and travel distances along the road network.

    Before you can analyze food access, you need a clean, consistent dataset of grocery store locations and basic access information. Public sources help: OpenStreetMap, for example, lists more than 60 food stores in the two cities. But they cannot tell you whether a store sells fresh produce or accepts SNAP benefits, and some entries may be out of date. This episode demonstrates how a team would check and complete that dataset with QField in the field and QGIS on a computer.

    Callout

    This is a demonstration

    You do not need to install anything or follow along on a phone. The goal is to understand the workflow and what good field data looks like. If you want to try QField yourself, see the box at the end of this episode.

    What the mapper collects

    • One point per grocery store, placed at the main public entrance
    • A standard set of attributes, chosen from dropdown lists
    • A photo of the storefront sign
    • A short note about anything unusual

    The result is a dataset ready for a food access analysis, such as the network analysis in the next episode.

    Project setup

    Before anyone goes out, the project leader prepares a project in QGIS that includes:

    • An offline basemap, so the map works without mobile data
    • The study area boundary for Lafayette and West Lafayette
    • An editable point layer called Grocery Stores, starting from the stores already listed in OpenStreetMap
    • A prebuilt data entry form with dropdown lists

    The project is then packaged for QField with the QFieldSync plugin in QGIS, and copied to each phone, either by cable or through QFieldCloud, QField’s optional online syncing service.

    Callout

    Why prepare the form in advance?

    Field collection fails when every person invents their own fields and categories. A prepared form keeps the dataset clean and ready to analyze.

    The data schema (what gets collected, and why)

    Field Type Why
    store_name Text Needed to identify stores and find duplicates
    store_type Dropdown Compare supermarkets with convenience stores and other types
    address Text Match the store to other datasets and verify its location
    city Dropdown Filter and report by city
    zip Text Summarize by ZIP code area
    snap_accepted Yes / No / Unknown Access for people using SNAP benefits
    wic_accepted Yes / No / Unknown An additional access signal
    produce_available Yes / No / Unknown A simple measure of healthy food availability
    hours_observed Text Hours matter for access, for example for night-shift workers
    verification Dropdown Whether the record was checked in the field, and when
    notes Text Keeps context without inventing new fields
    photo_1 Attachment Evidence for later checking
    Callout

    Why dropdowns matter

    If one person writes “EBT”, another writes “SNAP” and another writes “Yes”, the later analysis becomes messy. Dropdowns prevent this kind of category drift.

    Part 1: Opening the project and checking it is ready

    The mapper opens QField and runs a quick check:

    1. The basemap displays.
    2. The study area boundary loads.
    3. The Grocery Stores layer is visible and can be edited.

    This is the most common point of failure: missing layers, broken file paths or read-only layers are often discovered only after arriving at the first store.

    Part 2: The GPS rule

    The mapper waits for the GPS accuracy to settle, then applies a rule:

    • Preferred: record a point when the accuracy is better than 10 meters
    • If that is not possible: record it anyway and describe the problem in notes

    A store point that is 30 to 50 meters off can change whether it falls inside a service area or which road it is assigned to, especially near boundaries.

    Part 3: Recording a store

    Example A: a full-service supermarket

    What the mapper does:

    1. Stands at the main public entrance (the placement rule).
    2. If the store is already on the map, opens that point instead of creating a new one. Otherwise, creates one point for the store.
    3. Fills in the form:
      • store_name: as shown on the sign
      • store_type: Supermarket
      • snap_accepted: Yes (based on a posted sign)
      • wic_accepted: Unknown (no sign visible)
      • produce_available: Yes (produce section visible)
      • hours_observed: copied from the door
      • verification: Field verified, with the date
    4. Takes a storefront photo showing the store’s name and, if visible, its posted hours.

    Why the entrance? Entrances are consistent and repeatable, and they are what matters for walking distance. The center of a large building, or its parking lot, is much less meaningful for access.

    Example B: a small market or convenience store

    What changes in the form:

    • store_type might be Convenience or Small market
    • produce_available might be Unknown or No, depending on what is visible
    • The mapper does not assume SNAP or WIC without evidence

    “Unknown” is better than a guess. Guessing introduces systematic bias into the dataset.

    Part 4: Common problems

    Situation What the mapper does Why
    A point with the same store name is already nearby Edits the existing point instead of adding a new one Duplicates inflate store counts and distort access
    GPS accuracy is worse than 10 m Records the point anyway and notes it, for example “GPS about 22 m; placed at main entrance” Being open about error is better than false precision
    The store is closed or being renovated Records it, notes “Closed during visit”, and leaves uncertain fields as Unknown Whether a store is open affects real access
    The store is not in the starting data Adds a new point Public datasets miss stores, especially small ones
    A store on the map no longer exists Sets verification to “Not found” rather than deleting it Keeps a record of what was checked

    Part 5: Sync and check in QGIS

    Back at the computer, the mapper syncs the project and opens it in QGIS to check:

    1. Completeness: are the required fields filled in?
    2. Location: do points fall inside the study area, and none in impossible places?
    3. Duplicates: any points with the same name very close together?
    4. Photos: do they open, and do they match their records?

    Checking right away means you still remember what you saw. Waiting weeks turns fixable problems into permanent uncertainty.

    What good output looks like

    At the end of the demonstration, the dataset has:

    • One record per store, with no duplicates
    • Consistent categories, controlled by dropdowns
    • “Unknown” used where appropriate, instead of guesses
    • Photos that support checking
    • Notes that capture exceptions without creating new categories
    • A record of which stores were verified, and when

    This is the foundation you need before any food desert mapping begins.

    Challenge

    Look at the starting data

    The grocery stores used in the next episode came from OpenStreetMap. Open the file in QGIS (Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer, Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc.) with this address:

    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataCollection/main/data/grocery_stores.geojson

    Open its attribute table. Which fields from the schema above are present, and which would a field visit need to add?

    The file has store_name, store_type, address, city, osm_id, source and verification. Every record says “Not field verified”, and some have no address or no name. A field visit would add snap_accepted, wic_accepted, produce_available, hours_observed, notes and photos, fill in missing names and addresses, and update verification.

    Callout

    Want to try QField yourself?

    1. Install QField on your phone from https://qfield.org/ (Android, iOS) or on a computer.
    2. In QGIS, install the QFieldSync plugin (Plugins > Manage and Install Plugins).
    3. Build a small project with one editable point layer, set dropdowns in Layer Properties > Attributes Form (choose the Value Map widget), and package it with QFieldSync.
    4. Copy the package to your phone, or use QFieldCloud, and map a few places around you.

    The QField documentation walks through each step.

    Next

    In the next episode, we use grocery store points like these, together with the road network, to measure how far people must travel to reach a supermarket.

    Key Points
    • A clear scenario and a consistent schema make field data analyzable
    • Prepare the project and form in QGIS before going out, and package it with QFieldSync
    • Place points by a fixed rule, record GPS accuracy, and use “Unknown” instead of guessing
    • Check the data in QGIS as soon as possible after collection

    Content from Network Analysis for Grocery Access in QGIS

    Last updated on 2026-10-17 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 75 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do we move from grocery store points to an analysis of travel along roads?
    • How do shortest path and service area tools in QGIS answer different questions about access?
    • Why is network distance often better than straight-line distance for access studies?

    Objectives

    • Load grocery store, road and study area layers into QGIS from the web
    • Reproject layers to a projected coordinate system so that distances are in meters
    • Calculate shortest paths from one origin to every supermarket
    • Generate service areas that show which streets are within walking distance of a supermarket
    • Recognize data problems that break network analysis

    Overview

    In the previous episode, a team mapped grocery stores in the field with QField. In this episode, we use grocery store points with a road network to ask a new question:

    How accessible are grocery stores when movement is limited to the road network?

    This episode moves from data collection to analysis. Instead of treating distance as a straight line, we measure routes along streets.

    Imagine that a class, a community partner or a student group wants to know how easy it is to reach a supermarket from a residence hall, an apartment complex or a neighborhood. We will:

    1. prepare the grocery store and road data
    2. calculate routes from one starting point to every supermarket
    3. create service areas showing the streets within a chosen distance of a supermarket

    The data

    Three small files are stored in this lesson’s repository. You do not need to download them; QGIS reads them straight from the web.

    Layer Contents Source
    grocery_stores 64 food stores in and around Lafayette and West Lafayette: 17 supermarkets, 2 wholesale stores and 45 convenience stores OpenStreetMap contributors (Open Database License), October 2026
    roads 3,466 road segments covering both cities and a margin around them U.S. Census Bureau, TIGER/Line 2024
    study_area The city limits of Lafayette and West Lafayette U.S. Census Bureau, 2024 cartographic boundary files

    The store points stand in for data collected with QField. In a real project, the team would have verified them in the field first.

    Prerequisite

    Before you begin

    • QGIS installed (see Setup)
    • Basic familiarity with the QGIS interface, for example from the Data Visualization module’s “Getting Started with QGIS” episode

    Step 1: Load and inspect the layers

    1. Open QGIS and start a new project.

    2. Go to Layer > Add Layer > Add Vector Layer.

    3. For Source Type, choose Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc. and leave Type as HTTP/HTTPS/FTP.

    4. Paste the first address into URI, click Add, and repeat for the other two:

      https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataCollection/main/data/grocery_stores.geojson
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataCollection/main/data/roads.geojson
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpatialTurn/DataCollection/main/data/study_area.geojson

    5. Click Close. In the Layers panel, drag grocery_stores to the top so the points draw above the roads.

    6. Right-click grocery_stores and choose Open Attribute Table. Look at the fields: store_name, store_type, address, city, osm_id, source and verification.

    Before analyzing anything, look for problems:

    • duplicate points
    • stores outside the study area
    • stores with no name or address
    • roads that look disconnected from the rest
    Challenge

    Quick inspection

    Look at the map and the attribute table. What do you notice? Which kinds of data problems would most directly affect a network analysis?

    You may notice that six convenience stores, such as a Love’s travel stop, lie just outside the city limits. Stores like these should usually stay in an analysis, because city residents shop there too. (All 17 supermarkets are inside the city limits.) A few convenience stores have no name, and several stores have no address. Two Fresh Thyme points might look like duplicates, but they are two different stores, one in each city; check before deleting anything.

    The problems that most directly affect a network analysis are those that affect where a route starts or ends:

    • a store point placed far from any road
    • duplicate stores, which inflate the number of destinations
    • disconnected road segments, which break routes
    • layers in different coordinate systems, which appear in the wrong place

    Step 2: Keep only the supermarkets

    Convenience stores rarely sell a full range of fresh food, so food access studies usually focus on supermarkets.

    1. Open the Processing Toolbox (Processing > Toolbox).
    2. Search for Extract by attribute and open it.
    3. Set Input layer to grocery_stores, Selection attribute to store_type, Operator to =, and Value to Supermarket.
    4. Click Run. A new layer called Extracted (attribute) appears with 17 supermarkets. Rename it supermarkets (right-click > Rename Layer).

    Step 3: Reproject the data

    Network analysis should be done in a projected coordinate system, so that distances are measured in meters rather than degrees. The files are stored in latitude and longitude (EPSG:4326). For Lafayette, a good choice is NAD83 / UTM zone 16N (EPSG:26916).

    1. In the Processing Toolbox, search for Reproject layer and open it.
    2. Set Input layer to supermarkets and Target CRS to EPSG:26916.
    3. Click Run, and rename the output supermarkets_utm.
    4. Repeat for roads (rename the output roads_utm) and study_area (study_area_utm).
    5. Set the project coordinate system too: click the CRS button in the bottom-right corner of the QGIS window (it shows something like EPSG:4326), search for 26916, select NAD83 / UTM zone 16N, and click OK.
    Caution

    Why set the project CRS as well?

    QGIS’s network tools report travel cost in the units of the project’s coordinate system. If the project is still in EPSG:4326, a 4 km route is reported as a cost of about 0.036 (degrees). With the project in EPSG:26916, the same route has a cost of about 4,000 (meters).

    Do not assume that layers are ready for analysis just because they draw in the same place. Check the CRS of each layer (right-click > Properties > Information).

    Step 4: Do not clip the roads too tightly

    It is tempting to clip the road layer to the city limits to make it smaller. Here, that is a mistake. The road file already stops a short distance outside the two cities, and the city limits are irregular: they do not even meet each other across the Wabash River. Clipping the roads to them removes the bridges and splits the network into pieces.

    With the full road layer, all 17 supermarkets can be reached. With roads clipped to the city limits, only 7 can. When you do clip a network, clip it to a generous rectangle or buffer around your study area, never to an irregular boundary.

    Step 5: Choose a starting point

    Our origin is the Purdue Memorial Union, in the center of campus. You will set it inside the shortest path tool in the next step, either by clicking on the map or by typing its coordinates:

    507575, 4474900 [EPSG:26916]
    Discussion

    Why start with one origin?

    Why might it be better to start with a single origin before moving on to many homes or neighborhoods?

    A single origin keeps the first analysis easy to read. You can inspect the routes, compare stores and find problems with snapping or connectivity before moving to a more complex workflow with many origins.

    Step 6: Shortest paths to every supermarket

    1. In the Processing Toolbox, search for Shortest path (point to layer) and open it.
    2. Set the parameters:
      • Vector layer representing network: roads_utm
      • Path type to calculate: Shortest
      • Start point (x, y): click the … button, then click the Purdue Memorial Union on the map, or paste the coordinates from Step 5
      • Vector layer with end points: supermarkets_utm
      • Shortest path: leave as a temporary layer
      • Non-routable features: leave as a temporary layer
    3. Click Run.

    You now have a line layer, Shortest path, with one route from the origin to each supermarket. Its cost field is the route length in meters.

    Callout

    When a store cannot be reached

    If a store cannot be reached through the network, its route has an empty (NULL) cost. Stores that cannot be connected to the network at all are listed in the Non-routable features layer. Both usually point to a data problem: a store far from any road, a gap in the network, or a network clipped too tightly.

    Step 7: Compare network and straight-line distance

    1. Style the Shortest path layer with a bold, bright line, the supermarkets with a distinct point symbol, and the roads in light gray.
    2. Open the attribute table of Shortest path and click the Field Calculator button (the abacus icon).
    3. Create a new field route_km (Decimal number) with the expression "cost" / 1000.
    4. Create another field straight_km with the expression distance(start_point($geometry), end_point($geometry)) / 1000. This is the straight-line distance between the two ends of the route.
    5. Create a third field detour with the expression "route_km" / "straight_km".
    6. Close the Field Calculator, turn off editing (save the edits), and sort the table by route_km.

    The nearest supermarket by road is about 1.3 km away. On average, routes are about 14% longer than straight lines, and some are much longer: the Walmart Supercenter on Veterans Memorial Parkway is 8.0 km away in a straight line but about 10.1 km by road, a detour of about 1.3. The river, the few bridges, railroads and cul-de-sacs all force detours.

    Challenge

    Interpreting route results

    A store looks close on the map, but its route is much longer than expected. Name two possible reasons.

    • The street network requires a detour, for example because there is no bridge or direct road
    • The store or the origin snapped to a different road segment than you expected
    • Barriers such as rivers, railroads, highways with few crossings, or cul-de-sacs
    • The store point is slightly off its true entrance, for example in the middle of a large parking lot

    Step 8: Service areas around supermarkets

    Shortest paths answer the question: how do I get from one place to each store?

    Service areas answer a different question: which streets are within a given distance of a store?

    1. In the Processing Toolbox, search for Service area (from layer) and open it.
    2. Set the parameters:
      • Vector layer representing network: roads_utm
      • Vector layer with start points: supermarkets_utm
      • Path type to calculate: Shortest
      • Travel cost: 800 (meters, about a 10-minute walk)
    3. Click Run.

    The output, Service area (lines), shows the parts of the street network you can reach within 800 m of a supermarket.

    Only about 11% of the street length inside the two cities is within an 800 m walk of a supermarket. Most supermarkets sit on commercial corridors at the edges of the cities, designed for people who drive.

    Step 9: Interpret the results

    Service areas support questions such as:

    • Which parts of the study area appear well served by the current supermarkets?
    • Which neighborhoods appear poorly connected?
    • How does the answer change with a travel cost of 400 m, 800 m or 1,600 m?

    Combine this with the census map from the Census episode. Of the six census tracts with the highest share of households without a car, four (tracts 4, 7, 105 and 112, in central Lafayette and around the Purdue campus) have almost no streets within 800 m of a supermarket. That is exactly where a food access problem would be expected.

    Remember that the result is only as good as the network and the assumptions behind it:

    • A road centerline layer does not show sidewalks, crosswalks or footpaths
    • Highways appear walkable in the network, but are not
    • Verified store points improve the destinations, but cannot fix a poor road layer
    Discussion

    Reflection

    What parts of real-world access are still missing from this analysis, even after using a network instead of straight-line distance?

    Possible answers include sidewalk quality, crosswalks, traffic safety, bus routes, store hours, prices, food quality, disability access, and whether a road is really walkable.

    Challenge

    Change the distance

    Run Service area (from layer) again with a travel cost of 1600 (about a 20-minute walk). How does the picture change?

    The share of city streets within reach rises from about 11% to about 40%, and the green areas begin to join along the main corridors. But some areas are still left out: tract 105, beside the Purdue campus, where more than 40% of households have no car, has no streets within 1,600 m of a supermarket along the network. Walking 20 minutes each way with groceries is a real burden, which is why access studies also consider car ownership and public transit.

    Step 10: Save your outputs

    Temporary layers disappear when QGIS closes. To keep them, right-click each one and choose Export > Save Features As…, and save it to a GeoPackage (for example grocery_access.gpkg) with a different Layer name for each:

    • supermarkets_utm
    • roads_utm
    • shortest_paths
    • service_area_800m

    Then save the project (Project > Save). These outputs can be reused to join service areas to census data, to design a map layout, or to compare neighborhoods.

    Suggested pacing: loading and inspection 10 minutes; extracting and reprojecting 15; shortest paths 15; comparing distances 10; service areas 15; discussion and challenges 15.

    Teaching strategy: keep the lesson focused on one idea: network distance differs from straight-line distance. Connect it to the census episode’s map of households without a car.

    Common learner problems:

    • the project CRS is left in EPSG:4326, so costs appear in degrees
    • layers are not reprojected consistently
    • the road network is clipped too tightly (show the clipping figure)
    • learners confuse service areas with buffers (a buffer ignores roads)
    • outputs are left as temporary layers and lost

    Extensions: compare shortest and fastest paths; build a layer of several origins (residence halls or apartment complexes); convert service area lines to polygons with the Concave hull tool; join service areas to census tracts.

    Key Points
    • Grocery store points become far more useful for access questions when combined with a road network
    • Reproject layers and set the project CRS to a projected system so that costs are in meters
    • Shortest path tools compare routes; service area tools show which streets are within reach
    • Network distance is longer than straight-line distance, sometimes by much more than expected
    • Clipping a network to an irregular boundary can break routes; check for unreachable destinations
